rv.q: In Ian Rickson’s flawless production, it seems to expand to fill the vast space of the Olivier.
The depth and richness of this 1980 classic by Brian Friel are sounded beautifully in Ian Rickson’s magnificent revival in the Olivier.

Ian Rickson’s tremendous, generous and compendious new production of this singular classic invites us to consider the political landscape of Ireland in the 1830s and the move to start National schools.

It is a brilliant idea: understated enough that Friel can use it to deftly tell a bilingual story without surtitles or whatnot, but much deeper in its symbolism. It’s poignant that the Irish characters are speaking in English because the language of the colonisers would go on to swallow these people whole in just a generation or two.

This terrific, unfussy new production allows the audience to unpeel its own meaning, and the result is a simple but effective rendering of Friel’s lyrical, deeply moving work, focusing on the spoken word and the psychological realism of its characters.
This account of what’s perhaps his best play savours its rhythms, and that’s crucial, because at root it’s a vision of the power of language...

Particular credit, then, to Ian Rickson and his remarkably empathic team for steering Friel's complex weave of characters on to the National's largest, most exposing stage – the Olivier – and ensuring that it lands.

Translations is a perfectly constructed, immensely powerful and poetic work that receives an impeccable, beautifully acted production, which works on numerous levels and should provide a welcome sell-out success for the National Theatre this summer.
Excellently staged and acted, it may be a long production but it is worth every minute.

Its outline of bricks resembles a scattering of sandbags, with books propping up the parapet and wooden duckboards bridging the mud. This is the frontline in a war of words. Judith Roddy's Maire, who dreams of leaving for America, yearns to learn English to no avail: "The old language is a barrier to modern progress," she insists.
Ian Rickson's pedestrian production takes some time to warm up to, yet ends with a "do you see what I'm saying?" nod to how timely the piece is.
In this pitched-perfect National Theatre production in the Olivier though, Translations taps as close to its power as it can. This is the version for a generation.
The production is excellently acted by a fine ensemble, excellently directed by Ian Rickson and excellently designed by Rae Smith.
This is an empathetic, entertaining, relevant and moving revival of a modern classic.
Nevertheless, for much of its length it is magnificent.
It’s a daydream Ireland, brought to life with some finesse – the details include rainwater dripping into buckets from the top of the stage.
It’s well paced, allowing the individuality and emotional arc of the characters to emerge, and for the audience to care, while keep the momentum across the two and half hours that flies by.

cn.t: Friel's masterpiece receives a magnificent revival that fills the Olivier's vast space with beauty and resonance. Critics laud Rickson's flawless direction and the multilayered exploration of language, identity, and empire.
